steps.text: Castling is the only move where two pieces move at once: your king slides two squares toward a rook, and the rook hops over it. You can castle only if neither piece has moved, nothing is between them, and the king is not in check or crossing an attacked square.
Your turn: castle kingside. Move your king two squares to the right.
steps.hint: Select the king on e1, then tap g1.
steps.right: That's castling. Your king is safer and your rook is in play.

steps.text: En passant: if an enemy pawn jumps two squares and lands beside your pawn, you may capture it as if it had moved only one square. You must do it on your very next move or the chance is gone.
Black just played d7-d5. Capture that pawn en passant.
steps.hint: Your pawn on e5 captures diagonally to d6, the square the black pawn jumped over.
steps.right: Well done. The d5 pawn is removed even though your pawn lands on d6.

steps.text: Promotion: a pawn that reaches the last rank becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight (this app picks a queen). Push your pawn to promote it.
steps.hint: Move the pawn from e7 to e8.

steps.text: Back-rank mate: a king trapped behind its own pawns cannot step forward, so a rook or queen on the back rank gives checkmate.
Find the checkmate in one move.
steps.hint: Slide the rook all the way up the a-file.
steps.right: Checkmate. The black pawns blocked the king's own escape squares.

steps.text: The king and queen work as a team: the king takes away escape squares while the queen gives check. Find the checkmate in one.
steps.hint: Give check along the back rank.
steps.right: Mate! Your king covers g7 and h7, and the queen covers the rest.

steps.text: Now do it yourself: checkmate the black king. Use the queen to shrink the space around the king, then bring your own king closer. Careful: if the enemy king has no legal move but is not in check, it is stalemate, a draw.
steps.right: Checkmate! This is the most useful basic technique in chess.

Most games at this level are decided by hanging pieces: pieces nobody defends. Before every move ask two questions: what can my opponent capture right now, and what can I capture for free?
Black's queen is undefended and your knight attacks it. Take it!
steps.hint: Your knight on c3 attacks the queen.
steps.right: A free queen! Always check whether a piece is protected before capturing.

steps.text: A fork is one piece attacking two targets at once. Knights are brilliant at it because they jump and cannot be blocked.
Find the knight move that attacks both the black king and the rook.
steps.hint: Jump to the square that attacks both e8 and a8.
steps.right: Fork! The king must move, so you win the rook.

steps.text: Black has left something loose. Five positions: find the capture that wins material. Ask: what is attacked, and what is defended?
Find the capture that wins material.
Five positions where your knight wins material. Count attackers and defenders before you capture.
Win material with your knight.
Five positions where your bishop wins material. Count attackers and defenders before you capture.
Win material with your bishop.
Five positions where your rook wins material. Count attackers and defenders before you capture.
Win material with your rook.
Five positions with a knight fork: one jump that attacks two valuable pieces and cannot be captured.
Find the knight fork.
Three goals for the opening: 1) control the centre, 2) develop your knights and bishops, 3) castle to protect your king.
Start by claiming the centre with a pawn.
steps.hint: Push the pawn in front of your king or your queen two squares.
steps.right: Good. Centre pawns give your pieces room to move.

steps.text: Black copied you. Now develop a knight toward the centre.
steps.hint: Knights belong on c3 or f3, not on the edge.
steps.right: Developing a knight adds another piece fighting for the centre.

steps.text: Your king is still in the middle. Castle to safety.
steps.hint: Move the king two squares toward the h1 rook.
steps.right: Castled! Your king is safe and your rook is ready to join in.
